title: The Fox and the Grapes
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A hungry Fox saw some fine bunches of Grapes hanging from a vine that was trained along a high trellis, and did his best to reach them by jumping as high as he could into the air. But it was all in vain, for they were just out of reach: so he gave up trying, and walked away with an air of dignity and unconcern, remarking, "I thought those Grapes were ripe, but I see now they are quite sour."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the hungry Fox see hanging from the vine?
options: A cluster of ripe apples
A basket left by a farmer
Fine bunches of Grapes
A nest of small birds

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fox try to reach the Grapes?
options: By jumping as high as he could into the air
By climbing up the trellis itself
By asking another animal for help
By waiting for the grapes to fall

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Fox fail to reach the Grapes?
options: The vine collapsed before he could jump
A gust of wind blew them higher
Another fox had already eaten them
They were just out of reach

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Fox walk away after giving up?
options: Sulking and muttering to himself
With an air of dignity and unconcern
Running as fast as he could
Limping from the effort of jumping

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Fox say about the Grapes as he leaves?
options: That they were too high for any animal to reach
That he will come back for them tomorrow
That he now sees they are quite sour
That the vine was not worth the trouble

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Fox suddenly decide the Grapes are sour?
options: He is making an excuse to avoid admitting he simply couldn't reach them
He actually tastes one and finds it bitter
Another animal warns him the grapes are unripe
He notices they have begun to rot on the vine

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Fox's calm exit suggest about how he wants to appear?
options: As though he is furious at his own weakness
As though he plans to return with a ladder
As though he never wanted the grapes to begin with
As though the failure did not bother him at all

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "in vain" mean in "it was all in vain"?
options: Without warning
Without success
Without effort
Without witnesses

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "unconcern" mean in "an air of dignity and unconcern"?
options: A deep sense of pride
A feeling of great hunger
A lack of worry or care
A wish to try again later

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: People sometimes claim not to want what they cannot actually get
Foxes are naturally less agile than most other animals
Grapes grown on high trellises are rarely worth eating
Persistence always eventually leads to success

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how is the vine described as being trained?
options: Around a wooden fence
Over a low stone wall
Beside a running stream
Along a high trellis

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what condition is the Fox in at the start of the story?
options: Injured
Hungry
Sleepy
Frightened

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what word does the Fox use to describe the Grapes he originally hoped to eat?
options: "Sweet"
"Plentiful"
"Ripe"
"Fresh"

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Fox's remark about the Grapes be considered unconvincing?
options: He never actually tasted them, so he has no real basis for the claim
He had eaten similar grapes before and knew their taste well
He asked another fox to confirm they were sour first
The Grapes had visibly begun to rot on the vine

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Fox's changed opinion of the Grapes help him avoid feeling?
options: Fear of being caught near the vine
Guilt over damaging the vine while jumping
Embarrassment at being seen by another animal
Disappointment at failing to reach something he wanted

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "trellis" refer to in the passage?
options: A tool used to pick fruit
A frame that supports climbing plants
A type of woven basket
A path through a garden

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Fox successfully reaches the grapes after several attempts
A Fox shares the grapes with another hungry animal
A Fox fails to reach some grapes and then claims he never wanted them
A Fox is warned away from the grapes by their owner
